issues.legal_issue: A reference and award in a partition suit do not exceed the court’s jurisdiction over foreign immovable property when that property was excluded from the matters in dispute and the award merely recites an admitted position without determining title or effecting partition.
material_facts: The trial court’s preliminary decree excluded immovable properties situated outside its jurisdiction, and the finding concerning those properties was not challenged in the appeal brought by the claimant seeking partition.
The parties’ reference was made while appeals concerning other matters were pending; the foreign immovable properties were not then in dispute between them.

The award did not partition the properties abroad or determine the parties’ shares in them. It recited their position as divided branches and provided for the safekeeping of title documents until a partition could be made according to law.
The award similarly stated that the properties in the Indian State had not been divided and could be divided later.
issues.conclusion: The reference and award were not invalid on the ground that they dealt with foreign immovable properties beyond the court’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: A court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate title to, or direct the division of, immovable property situated in a foreign country. But a mere recital of an existing fact or admitted legal position is distinct from a determination that creates or declares title. The Court relied on the distinction stated in Bageshwari Charan Singh v. Jagarnath Kuari (1932) and on the rule stated in Dicey’s Conflict of Laws.

predicates.partition_suit_with_foreign_immovables: The proceeding seeks division of family property and includes immovable property situated outside the deciding court’s territorial jurisdiction.
predicates.foreign_property_excluded_from_live_disp: The court excluded the foreign immovable property from its decree, and no party kept its treatment in dispute in the pending proceedings.
predicates.award_only_recites_admitted_position: The decision-maker did not partition the foreign property or determine title to it, but only recorded the parties’ existing position or made a custodial arrangement pending a future lawful partition.

issues.definition: When a partition proceeding concerns foreign immovable property that is no longer in dispute, an award that only records an admitted position about it does not make the foreign-property objection succeed.

issues.legal_issue: A reference to arbitration and an award do not breach a stay that prohibits only the drawing of a final decree while permitting further proceedings in the partition suit.
material_facts: The appellate court ordered that a final decree not be drawn while the appeals were pending, but did not stay all proceedings before the commissioner.
The parties later referred their disputes to arbitrators, whose proceedings substantially corresponded to the inquiry that the commissioner would otherwise have conducted.
The award was not itself a final decree.
issues.conclusion: The reference and award did not contravene the appellate court’s stay order.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of a stay is determined by what the order actually prohibits. An order preventing the drawing of a final decree does not prohibit an inquiry or other proceedings that remain permitted, and an award that is not a final decree does not violate that restriction.

rule.if: partition_suit_with_limited_stay and stay_only_bars_final_decree and further_inquiry_permitted and award_is_not_final_decree

predicates.partition_suit_with_limited_stay: The proceeding is a partition suit in which an interim order restricts some, but not all, further steps.
predicates.stay_only_bars_final_decree: The court’s order prohibits drawing a final decree while the matter is pending, without staying all other proceedings.
predicates.further_inquiry_permitted: The order leaves an inquiry or comparable further proceeding available to be conducted.
predicates.award_is_not_final_decree: The decision made through the reference is not itself a final decree in the suit.

issues.definition: Where a limited stay bars only a final decree and permits further inquiry, an award that is not a final decree does not breach the stay.

issues.legal_issue: The terms “court” and “suit” in section 21 of the Arbitration Act include an appellate court and appellate proceedings that continue the suit.
material_facts: The parties jointly sought a reference while appeals from the preliminary decree were pending.
The matters raised in the appeals remained matters in difference between the parties in the suit.
The appellate court could affect the nature and effect of the decree under appeal, and the trial court and appellate court had the powers described in section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: Section 21 permits a reference to arbitration during appellate proceedings, and its references to a court and a suit include the appellate court and those proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 applies when all interested parties agree to refer a matter in difference in the suit before judgment is pronounced. Since an appeal is a continuation of the suit and the appellate court generally has the powers of the trial court under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure, “court” and “suit” in section 21 include the appellate court and appellate proceedings. Section 41 of the Arbitration Act is consistent with this construction. The Court disapproved Abani Bhusan Chakravarty v. Hem Chandra Chakravarty and approved Thakur Prasad v. Baleshwar Ahir, Moradhwaj v. Bhudar Das, and Subramannaya Bhatta v. Devadas Nayak.

predicates.arbitration_reference_in_pending_appeal: The parties seek a reference to arbitration while an appeal concerning their suit is pending.
predicates.all_interested_parties_agree: Every party interested in the suit agrees in writing to refer the matter to arbitration.
predicates.appellate_issues_remain_in_dispute: The appeal continues to raise matters in difference between the parties in the suit.

issues.definition: When all interested parties agree to arbitrate matters still disputed in a pending appeal, the appellate court and appeal fall within the scope of a reference under the provision.

issues.legal_issue: For a reference under section 21, “judgment” means a judgment finally deciding all matters in controversy, and a judgment followed by a preliminary decree in a partition suit is not final.
material_facts: The trial court had delivered judgment and made a preliminary decree in the partition suit.
Further proceedings to work out the partition and pass a final decree remained pending when the parties sought arbitration.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary decree did not prevent a reference under section 21 because the suit had not reached final judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 permits an application for reference before judgment is pronounced. In that section, judgment means one finally deciding all matters in controversy, not an interlocutory decision. A partition suit continues after a preliminary decree until the final decree; the Court relied on Jadu Nath Roy v. Parameswar Mullick.

predicates.partition_suit_with_preliminary_decree: The proceeding is a partition suit in which the court has made a preliminary decree.
predicates.final_decree_proceedings_remain: Further proceedings are still required to complete the partition and make a final decree.
predicates.parties_apply_before_final_disposition: The parties seek the reference before the court finally disposes of the suit.

issues.definition: If a preliminary decree has been made in a partition suit but proceedings to complete the suit remain, an application made before final disposition is not barred by the preliminary decree.

issues.legal_issue: When a preliminary decree is under appeal and further proceedings remain before the trial court, either the trial court or the appellate court may refer all matters in dispute to arbitration.
material_facts: A preliminary decree had been made and appeals against it were pending before the appellate court.
Proceedings subsequent to the preliminary decree, including steps toward a final decree, remained before the trial court.
The disputes in the appeals and the further trial-court proceedings were connected, and the parties jointly sought one reference covering all matters in dispute.
issues.conclusion: Either court could make a reference covering all matters in dispute; because post-decree proceedings were pending before the trial court, that court was competent to make the reference in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940, when a preliminary decree is under appeal, some matters in dispute are before the appellate court and subsequent proceedings remain before the trial court. Because those matters may be closely connected and effective arbitration may require one reference, either court may refer all matters in dispute. The trial court had jurisdiction here because post-decree proceedings were pending before it.

rule.if: partition_suit_with_preliminary_decree_appeal and trial_court_proceedings_remain and appellate_matters_remain_pending and all_interested_parties_agree

predicates.partition_suit_with_preliminary_decree_a: The proceeding is a partition suit in which an appeal has been brought against a preliminary decree.
predicates.trial_court_proceedings_remain: Further proceedings under the preliminary decree remain pending before the trial court.
predicates.appellate_matters_remain_pending: Matters in dispute under the preliminary decree remain pending before the appellate court.
predicates.all_interested_parties_agree: Every party interested in the suit agrees to refer the matters in dispute to arbitration.

issues.definition: When a preliminary decree in a partition suit is under appeal, further trial-court proceedings remain, and all interested parties agree, either court may refer all connected disputes to arbitration.
